entries.bd78dfeee92c9f000891ba8eab72ec576c0b3384: <div sID="gen10920" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="32" osisID="Ps.32" sID="Ps.32"/> <div eID="gen10920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10921" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10922" type="x-p"/> This psalm, though it speaks not of Christ, as many of the psalms we have hitherto met with have done, has yet a great deal of gospel in it. The apostle tells us that David, in this psalm, describes "the blessedness of the man unto whom God imputes righteousness without words," <reference osisRef="Rom.4.6">Rom. iv. 6</reference>. We have here a summary, I. Of gospel grace in the pardon of sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), in divine protection (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.7">ver. 7</reference>), and divine guidance, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">ver. 8</reference>. II. Of gospel duty. To confess sin (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.3-Ps.32.5">ver. 3-5</reference>), to pray (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">ver. 6</reference>), to govern ourselves well (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.9-Ps.32.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>), and to rejoice in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.11">ver. 11</reference>. The way to obtain these privileges is to make conscience of these duties, which we ought to think of—of the former for our comfort, of the latter for our quickening, when we sing this psalm. Grotius thinks it was designed to be sung on the day of atonement.
entries.399f0a44bb9f43ef64f9169dddf0592508230f11: <div eID="gen10922" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10921" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Who Are Blessed.</title> <div sID="gen10923" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is he whose</hi> transgression <hi type="italic">is</hi> forgiven, <hi type="italic">whose</hi> sin <hi type="italic">is</hi> covered. <hi type="super">2</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man unto whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> imputeth not iniquity, and in whose spirit <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no guile. <hi type="super">3</hi> When I kept silence, my bones waxed old through my roaring all the day long. <hi type="super">4</hi> For day and night thy hand was heavy upon me: my moisture is turned into the drought of summer. Selah. <hi type="super">5</hi> I acknowledged my sin unto thee, and mine iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; and thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin. Selah. <hi type="super">6</hi> For this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee in a time when thou mayest be found: surely in the floods of great waters they shall not come nigh unto him. <div eID="gen10923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10924" type="x-p"/> This psalm is entitled <hi type="italic">Maschil,</hi> which some take to be only the name of the tune to which it was set and was to be sung. But others think it is significant; our margin reads it, <hi type="italic">A psalm of David giving instruction,</hi> and there is nothing in which we have more need of instruction than in the nature of true blessedness, wherein it consists and the way that leads to it—what we must do that we may be happy. There are several things in which these verses instruct us. In general, we are here taught that our happiness consists in the favour of God, and not in the wealth of this world—in spiritual blessings, and not the good things of this world. When David says (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Ps. i. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Blessed is the man that walks not in the counsel of the ungodly,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.1">Ps. cxix. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">Blessed are the undefiled in the way,</hi> the meaning is, "This is the character of the blessed man; and he that has not this character cannot expect to be happy:" but when it is here said, <hi type="italic">Blessed is the man whose iniquity is forgiven,</hi> the meaning is, "This is the ground of his blessedness: this is that fundamental privilege from which all the other ingredients of his blessedness flow." In particular, we are here instructed, <div eID="gen10924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10925" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning the nature of the pardon of sin. This is that which we all need and are undone without; we are therefore concerned to be very solicitous and inquisitive about it. 1. It is the forgiving of transgression. <hi type="italic">Sin is the transgression of the law.</hi> Upon our repentance, the transgression is forgiven; that is, the obligation to punishment which we lay under, by virtue of the sentence of the law, is vacated and cancelled; it is <hi type="italic">lifted off</hi> (so some read it), that by the pardon of it we may be eased of a burden, a heavy burden, like a load on the back, that makes us stoop, or a load on the stomach, that makes us sick, or a load on the spirits, that makes us sink. The remission of sins gives rest and relief to those that were <hi type="italic">weary and heavily laden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Matt. xi. 28</reference>. 2. It is the covering of sin, as nakedness is covered, that it may not appear to our shame, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Rev. iii. 18</reference>. One of the first symptoms of guilt in our first parents was blushing at their own nakedness. Sin makes us loathsome in the sight of God and utterly unfit for communion with him, and, when conscience is awakened, it makes us loathsome to ourselves too; but, when sin is pardoned, it is covered with the robe of Christ's righteousness, like the coats of skins wherewith God clothed Adam and Eve (an emblem of the remission of sins), so that God is no longer displeased with us, but perfectly reconciled. They are not covered from us (no; <hi type="italic">My sin is ever before me</hi>) nor covered from God's omniscience, but from his vindictive justice. When he pardons sin he <hi type="italic">remembers it no more,</hi> he <hi type="italic">casts it behind his back,</hi> it <hi type="italic">shall be sought for and not found,</hi> and the sinner, being thus reconciled to God, begins to be reconciled to himself. 3. It is the not imputing of iniquity, not laying it to the sinner's charge, not proceeding against him for it according to the strictness of the law, not dealing with him as he deserves. The righteousness of Christ being imputed to us, and we being made <hi type="italic">the righteousness of God in him,</hi> our iniquity is not imputed, God having <hi type="italic">laid upon him the iniquity of us all</hi> and made him <hi type="italic">sin for us.</hi> Observe, Not to impute iniquity is God's act, for he is the Judge. <hi type="italic">It is God that justifies.</hi> <div eID="gen10925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10926" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning the character of those whose sins are pardoned: <hi type="italic">in whose spirit there is no guile.</hi> He does not say, "There is no <hi type="italic">guilt</hi>" (for who is there that lives and sins not?), but no <hi type="italic">guile;</hi> the pardoned sinner is one that does not dissemble with God in his professions of repentance and faith, nor in his prayers for peace or pardon, but in all these is sincere and means as he says—that does not repent with a purpose to sin again, and then sin with a purpose to repent again, as a learned interpreter glosses upon it. Those that design honestly, that are really what they profess to be, are Israelites indeed, in whom is no guile. <div eID="gen10926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10927" type="x-p"/> III. Concerning the happiness of a justified state: <hi type="italic">Blessednesses are to the man whose iniquity is forgiven,</hi> all manner of blessings, sufficient to make him completely blessed. That is taken away which incurred the curse and obstructed the blessing; and then God will pour out blessings till there be no room to receive them. The forgiveness of sin is that article of the covenant which is the reason and ground of all the rest. <hi type="italic">For I will be merciful to their unrighteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.8.12">Heb. viii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen10927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10928" type="x-p"/> IV. Concerning the uncomfortable condition of an unhumbled sinner, that sees his guilt, but is not yet brought to make a penitent confession of it. This David describes very pathetically, from his own sad experience (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.3-Ps.32.4">v. 3, 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">While I kept silence my bones waxed old.</hi> Those may be said to keep silence who stifle their convictions, who, when they cannot but see the evil of sin and their danger by reason of it, ease themselves by not thinking of it and diverting their minds to something else, as Cain to the building of a city,—who <hi type="italic">cry not when God binds them,</hi>—who will not unburden their consciences by a penitent confession, nor seek for peace, as they ought, by faithful and fervent prayer,—and who choose rather to pine away in their iniquities than to take the method which God has appointed of finding rest for their souls. Let such expect that their smothered convictions will be a fire in their bones, and the wounds of sin, not opened, will fester, and grow intolerably painful. If conscience be seared, the case is so much the more dangerous; but if it be startled and awake, it will be heard. The hand of divine wrath will be felt lying heavily upon the soul, and the anguish of the spirit will affect the body; to the degree David experienced it, so that when he was young his bones waxed old; and even his silence made him <hi type="italic">roar all the day long,</hi> as if he had been under some grievous pain and distemper of body, when really the cause of all his uneasiness was the struggle he felt in his own bosom between his convictions and his corruptions. Note, <hi type="italic">He that covers his sin shall not prosper;</hi> some inward trouble is required in repentance, but there is much worse in impenitency. <div eID="gen10928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10929" type="x-p"/> V. Concerning the true and only way to peace of conscience. We are here taught to confess our sins, that they may be forgiven, to declare them, that we may be justified. This course David took: <hi type="italic">I acknowledged my sin unto thee,</hi> and no longer <hi type="italic">hid my iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.5">v. 5</reference>. Note, Those that would have the comfort of the pardon of their sins must take shame to themselves by a penitent confession of them. We must confess the fact of sin, and be particular in it (<hi type="italic">Thus and thus have I done</hi>), confess the fault of sin, aggravate it, and lay a load upon ourselves for it (<hi type="italic">I have done very wickedly</hi>), confess the justice of the punishment we have been under for it (<hi type="italic">The Lord is just in all that is brought upon us</hi>), and that we deserve much worse—<hi type="italic">I am no more worthy to be called thy son.</hi> We must confess sin with shame and holy blushing, with fear and holy trembling. <div eID="gen10929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10930" type="x-p"/> VI. Concerning God's readiness to pardon sin to those who truly repent of it: "<hi type="italic">I said, I will confess</hi> (I sincerely resolved upon it, hesitated no longer, but came to a point, that I would make a free and ingenuous confession of my sins) <hi type="italic">and</hi> immediately <hi type="italic">thou forgavest the iniquity of my sin,</hi> and gavest me the comfort of the pardon in my own conscience; immediately I found rest to my soul." Note, God is more ready to pardon sin, upon our repentance, than we are to repent in order to the obtaining of pardon. It was with much ado that David was here brought to confess his sins; he was put to the rack before he was brought to do it (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.3-Ps.32.4">v. 3, 4</reference>), he held out long, and would not surrender till it came to the last extremity; but, when he did offer to surrender, see how quickly, how easily, he obtained good terms: "I did but say, <hi type="italic">I will confess, and thou forgavest.</hi>" Thus the father of the prodigal saw his returning son <hi type="italic">when he was yet afar off,</hi> and ran to meet him with the kiss that sealed his pardon. What an encouragement is this to poor penitents, and what an assurance does it give us that, <hi type="italic">if we confess our sins,</hi> we shall find God, not only <hi type="italic">faithful and just,</hi> but gracious and kind, <hi type="italic">to forgive us our sins!</hi> <div eID="gen10930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10931" type="x-p"/> VII. Concerning the good use that we are to make of the experience David had had of God's readiness to forgive his sins (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">For this shall every one that is godly pray unto thee.</hi> Note, 1. All godly people are praying people. As soon as ever Paul was converted, <hi type="italic">Behold, he prays,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.11">Acts ix. 11</reference>. You may as soon find a living man without breath as a living Christian without prayer. 2. The instructions given us concerning the happiness of those whose sins are pardoned, and the easiness of obtaining the pardon, should engage and encourage us to pray, and particularly to pray, <hi type="italic">God be merciful to us sinners.</hi> For this shall every one that is well inclined be earnest with God in prayer, and <hi type="italic">come boldly to the throne of grace,</hi> with hopes to <hi type="italic">obtain mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.16">Heb. iv. 16</reference>. 3. Those that would speed in prayer must seek the Lord in <hi type="italic">a time when he will be found.</hi> When, by his providence, he calls them to seek him, and by his Spirit stirs them up to seek him, they must <hi type="italic">go speedily to seek the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.8.21">Zech. viii. 21</reference>) and lose no time, lest death cut them off, and then it will be too late to seek him, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6">Isa. lv. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Behold, now is the accepted time,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2 Cor. vi. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.4">4</reference>. Those that are sincere and abundant in prayer will find the benefit of it when they are in trouble: <hi type="italic">Surely in the floods of great waters,</hi> which are very threatening, <hi type="italic">they shall not come nigh them,</hi> to terrify them, or create them any uneasiness, much less shall they overwhelm them. Those that have God <hi type="italic">nigh unto them in all that which they call upon him for,</hi> as all upright, penitent, praying people have, are so guarded, so advanced, that no waters—no, not great waters—no, not floods of them, can come nigh them, to hurt them. As the temptations of the <hi type="italic">wicked one touch them not</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.5.18">1 John v. 18</reference>), so neither do the troubles of this evil world; these fiery darts of both kinds, drop short of them.
entries.a67fd09b7a559d77ca04000fa78d6a1450c07527: <div eID="gen10931" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Devout Confidence.</title> <div sID="gen10932" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah. <hi type="super">8</hi> I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye. 9 Be ye not as the horse, <hi type="italic">or</hi> as the mule, <hi type="italic">which</hi> have no understanding: whose mouth must be held in with bit and bridle, lest they come near unto thee. <hi type="super">10</hi> Many sorrows <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> to the wicked: but he that trusteth in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , mercy shall compass him about. 11 Be glad in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and rejoice, ye righteous: and shout for joy, all <hi type="italic">ye that are</hi> upright in heart. <div eID="gen10932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10933" type="x-p"/> David is here improving the experience he had had of the comfort of pardoning mercy. <div eID="gen10933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10934" type="x-p"/> I. He speaks to God, and professes his confidence in him and expectation from him, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.7">v. 7</reference>. Having tasted the sweetness of divine grace to a penitent sinner, he cannot doubt of the continuance of that grace to a praying saint, and that in that grace he should find both safety and joy. 1. Safety: "<hi type="italic">Thou art my hiding-place;</hi> when by faith I have recourse to thee I see all the reason in the world to be easy, and to think myself out of the reach of any real evil. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt preserve me from trouble,</hi> from the sting of it, and from the strokes of it as far as is good for me. <hi type="italic">Thou shalt preserve me from</hi> such trouble as I was in <hi type="italic">while I kept silence,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.32.3">v. 3</reference>. When God has pardoned our sins, if he leaves us to ourselves, we shall soon run as far in debt again as ever and plunge ourselves again into the same gulf; and therefore, when we have received the comfort of our remission, we must fly to the grace of God to be preserved from returning to folly again, and having our hearts again hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. God keeps his people from trouble by keeping them from sin. 2. Joy: "Thou shalt not only deliver me, but <hi type="italic">compass me about with songs of deliverance;</hi> which way soever I look I shall see occasion to rejoice and to praise God; and my friends also shall compass me about in the great congregation, to join with me in songs of praise: they shall join their songs of deliverance with mine. As <hi type="italic">every one that is godly shall pray with me,</hi> so they shall give thanks with me." <div eID="gen10934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10935" type="x-p"/> II. He turns his speech to the children of men. Being himself converted, he does what he can to <hi type="italic">strengthen his brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.32">Luke xxii. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will instruct thee,</hi> whoever thou art that desirest instruction, <hi type="italic">and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">v. 8</reference>. This, in another of his penitential psalms, he resolves that when God should have restored to him the joy of his salvation he would teach transgressors his ways, and do what he could to convert sinners to God, as well as to comfort those that were converted, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.12-Ps.51.13">Ps. li. 12, 13</reference>. When Solomon became a penitent he immediately became a preacher, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.1">Eccl. i. 1</reference>. Those are best able to teach others the grace of God who have themselves had the experience of it: and those who are themselves taught of God ought to <hi type="italic">tell others what he has done for their souls</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>) and so teach them. <hi type="italic">I will guide thee with my eye.</hi> Some apply this to God's conduct and direction. He teaches us by his word and guides us with his eye, by the secret intimations of his will in the hints and turns of Providence, which he enables his people to understand and take direction from, as a master makes a servant know his mind by a wink of his eye. When Christ turned and looked upon Peter he guided him with his eye. But it is rather to be taken as David's promise to those who sat under his instruction, his own children and family especially: "<hi type="italic">I will counsel thee; my eye shall be upon thee</hi>" (so the margin reads it); "I will give thee the best counsel I can and then observe whether thou takest it or no." Those that are taught in the word should be under the constant inspection of those that teach them; spiritual guides must be overseers. In this application of the foregoing doctrine concerning the blessedness of those whose sins are pardoned we have a word to sinners and a word to saints; and this is rightly dividing the word of truth and giving to each their portion. <div eID="gen10935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10936" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is a word of caution to sinners, and a good reason is given for it. (1.) The caution is, not to be unruly and ungovernable: <hi type="italic">Be you not as the horse and the mule, which have no understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">v. 9</reference>. When the psalmist would reproach himself for the sins he repented of he compared himself to a <hi type="italic">beast before God</hi> (<hi type="italic">so foolish have I been and ignorant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.22">Ps. lxxiii. 22</reference>) and therefore warns others not to be so. It is our honour and happiness that we have understanding, that we are capable of being governed by reason and of reasoning with ourselves. Let us therefore use the faculties we have, and act rationally. The horse and mule must be managed <hi type="italic">with bit and bridle, lest they come near</hi> us, to do us a mischief, or (as some read it) that they may come near to us, to do us service, that they <hi type="italic">may obey us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.3">Jam. iii. 3</reference>. Let us not be like them; let us not be hurried by appetite and passion, at any time, to go contrary to the dictate of right reason and to our true interest. If sinners would be governed and determined by these, they would soon become saints and would not go a step further in their sinful courses; where there is renewing grace there is no need of the bit and bridle of restraining grace. (2.) The reason for this caution is because the way of sin which we would persuade you to forsake will certainly end in sorrow (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many sorrows shall be to the wicked,</hi> which will not only spoil their vain and carnal mirth, and put an end to it, but will make them pay dearly for it. Sin will have sorrow, if not repented of, everlasting sorrow. It was part of the sentence, <hi type="italic">I will greatly multiply thy sorrows.</hi> "Be wise for yourselves therefore, and turn from your wickedness, that you may prevent those sorrows, those many sorrows." <div eID="gen10936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10937" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is a word of comfort to saints, and a good reason is given for that too. (1.) They are assured that if they will but trust in the Lord, and keep closely to him, <hi type="italic">mercy shall compass them about</hi> on every side (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.10">v. 10</reference>), so that they shall not depart from God, for that mercy shall keep them in, nor shall any real evil break in upon them, for that mercy shall keep it out. (2.) They are therefore commanded to <hi type="italic">be glad in the Lord, and</hi> to <hi type="italic">rejoice</hi> in him, to such a degree as even to <hi type="italic">shout for joy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.32.11">v. 11</reference>. Let them be so transported with this holy joy as not to be able to contain themselves; and let them affect others with it, that they also may see that a life of communion with God is the most pleasant and comfortable life we can live in this world. This is that present bliss which the upright in heart, and they are only, are entitled to and qualified for.  <chapter eID="Ps.32"/> <div eID="gen10937" type="x-p"/>

The Psalmist describes the blessings of His forgiveness, succeeding the pains of conviction, and deduces from his own experience instruction and exhortation to others.</title> <div sID="gen8825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5799"/>1-2. entries.82abdd5505d1239d62d3c6ae5a13c4b5983139e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5807"/><div sID="gen8842" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5807"/>9. The latter clause, more literally, "in that they come not near thee"; that is, because they will not come, &c., unless forced by bit and bridle. <div eID="gen8842" type="x-p"/>
entries.87c8c6e8b9e36d1eff73aa642a59d014d76a685d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5808"/><div sID="gen8843" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5808"/>10. The sorrows of the impenitent contrasted with the peace and safety secured by God's mercy. <div eID="gen8843" type="x-p"/>
entries.2be851842da522c2a11bc0f9720a18e17841f3fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5809"/><div sID="gen8844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5809"/>11. entries.c5b493d7733f019a02bc2a289854a08150f5fc17: <div eID="gen19582" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19583" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19584" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19584" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19583" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19585" type="x-p"/> True blessedness consists in remission of sin, and purification of the heart, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.2">Psa 32:2</reference>. What the psalmist felt in seeking these blessings, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.3-Psa.32.5">Psa 32:3-5</reference>. How they should be sought, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.7">Psa 32:7</reference>. The necessity of humility and teachableness, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.8">Psa 32:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.9">Psa 32:9</reference>. The misery of the wicked, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.10">Psa 32:10</reference>. The blessedness of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Psa.32.11">Psa 32:11</reference>. <div eID="gen19585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19586" type="x-p"/> The title of this Psalm is significant, לדוד משכיל ledavid maskil, A Psalm of David, giving instruction, an instructive Psalm; so called by way of eminence, because it is calculated to give the highest instruction relative to the guilt of sin, and the blessedness of pardon and holiness or justification and sanctification. It is supposed to have been composed after David's transgression with Bath-sheba, and subsequently to his obtaining pardon. The Syriac entitles it, "A Psalm of David concerning the sin of Adam, who dared and transgressed; and a prophecy concerning Christ, because through him we are to be delivered from hell." The Arabic says, "David spoke this Psalm prophetically concerning the redemption." The Vulgate, Septuagint, and Ethiopic, are the same in meaning as the Hebrew. <div eID="gen19586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19587" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19588" type="x-p"/> Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven - In this and the following verse four evils are mentioned: <div eID="gen19588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19589" type="x-p"/> 1. Transgression, פשע peshwa. <div eID="gen19589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19590" type="x-p"/> 2. Sin, חטאה chataah. <div eID="gen19590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19591" type="x-p"/> 3. Iniquity, עון avon. <div eID="gen19591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19592" type="x-p"/> 4. Guile, רמיה remiyah. <div eID="gen19592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19593" type="x-p"/> The first signifies the passing over a boundary, doing what is prohibited. The second signifies the missing of a mark, not doing what was commanded; but is often taken to express sinfulness, or sin in the future, producing transgression in the life. The third signifies what is turned out of its proper course or situation; any thing morally distorted or perverted. Iniquity, what is contrary to equity or justice. The fourth signifies fraud, deceit, guile, etc. To remove these evils, three acts are mentioned: forgiving, covering, and not imputing. <div eID="gen19593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19594" type="x-p"/> 1. Transgression, פשע pesha, must be forgiven, נשוי nesui, borne away, i.e., by a vicarious sacrifice; for bearing sin, or bearing away sin, always implies this. <div eID="gen19594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19595" type="x-p"/> 2. Sin, חטאה chataah, must be covered, כסוי kesui, hidden from the sight. It is odious and abominable, and must be put out of sight. <div eID="gen19595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19596" type="x-p"/> 3. Iniquity, עון anon, which is perverse or distorted, must not be imputed, לא יחשב lo yachshob, must not be reckoned to his account. <div eID="gen19596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19597" type="x-p"/> 4. Guile, רמיה remiyah, must be annihilated from the soul: In whose spirit there is no Guile. The man whose transgression is forgiven; whose sin is hidden, God having cast it as a millstone into the depths of the sea; whose iniquity and perversion is not reckoned to his account; and whose guile, the deceitful and desperately wicked heart, is annihilated, being emptied of sin and filled with righteousness, is necessarily a happy man. <div eID="gen19597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19598" type="x-p"/> The old Psalter translates these two verses thus: Blissid qwas wikednes es for gyven, and qwas synnes is hyled (covered). Blisful man til qwam Lord retted (reckoneth) noght Syn: ne na treson es in his gast (spirit). In vain does any man look for or expect happiness while the power of sin remains, its guilt unpardoned, and its impurity not purged away. To the person who has got such blessings, we may say as the psalmist said, אשרי ashrey, O the blessedness of that man, whose transgression is forgiven! etc. <div eID="gen19598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19599" type="x-p"/> St. Paul quotes this passage, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.6-Rom.4.7">Rom 4:6-7</reference> (note), to illustrate the doctrine of justification by faith; where see the notes.
entries.8348990c7c641586429495a795a59d3638471a07: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19600" type="x-p"/> When I kept silence - Before I humbled myself, and confessed my sin, my soul was under the deepest horror. "I roared all the day long;" and felt the hand of God heavy upon my soul.
entries.b158041924442d038a9340f519d942eea9301feb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19601" type="x-p"/> I acknowledged my sin - When this confession was made thoroughly and sincerely, and I ceased to cover and extenuate my offense, then thou didst forgive the iniquity of my sin. I felt the hardness of heart: I felt the deep distress of soul; I felt power to confess and abhor my sin; I felt confidence in the mercy of the Lord; and I felt the forgiveness of the iniquity of my sin. <div eID="gen19601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19602" type="x-p"/> Selah - This is all true; I know it; I felt it; I feel it.
entries.08e39010cb66d9df58c3b95d587f4bbf6e7993f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen19602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19603" type="x-p"/> For this shall every one that is godly - Because thou art merciful; because thou hast shown mercy to all who have truly turned to thee, and believed in thee; every one who fears thee, and hears of this, shall pray unto thee in an acceptable time, when thou mayest be found; in the time of finding. When the heart is softened and the conscience alarmed, that is a time of finding. God is ever ready; men are not so. Who can pray with a hard heart and a dark mind? While you feel relentings, pray. <div eID="gen19603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19604" type="x-p"/> Surely in the floods - In violent trials, afflictions, and temptations; when the rains descend, the winds blow, and the floods beat against that godly man who prays and trusts in God; "they shall not come nigh him," so as to weaken his confidence or destroy his soul. His house is founded on a rock.
entries.7b7f4e43522f6178785f93608881933284d1682f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19605" type="x-p"/> Thou art my hiding place - An allusion, probably, to the city of refuge: "Thou shalt preserve me from trouble." The avenger of blood shall not be able to overtake me. And being encompassed with an impregnable wall, I shall feel myself encompassed with songs of deliverance - I shall know that I am safe.
entries.b1715f4ce7b36bc2870bd541e86b65066f8670c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19606" type="x-p"/> I will instruct thee - These are probably the Lord's words to David. Seeing thou art now sensible of the mercy thou hast received from me, and art purposing to live to my glory, I will give thee all the assistance requisite. I will become thy Instructor, "and will teach thee," in all occurrences, "the way thou shouldst go." I will keep mine eyes upon thee, and thou shalt keep thine upon me: as I go, thou must follow me; and I will continually watch for thy good.
entries.1a98fa5b3a5c9e3a028b0d53b89af772cd887f95: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19607" type="x-p"/> Be ye not as the horse or as the mule - They will only act by force and constraint; be not like them; give a willing service to your Maker. "They have no understanding;" you have a rational soul, made to be guided and influenced by reason. The service of your God is a reasonable service; act, therefore, as a rational being. The horse and the mule are turned with difficulty; they must be constrained with bit and bridle. Do not be like them; do not oblige your Maker to have continual recourse to afflictions, trials, and severe dispensations of providence, to keep you in the way, or to recover you after you have gone out of it.
entries.623254cbdad3ff4fc79b0238db42029a95dd3409: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen19607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19608" type="x-p"/> Many sorrows shall be to the wicked - Every wicked man is a miserable man. God has wedded sin and misery as strongly as he has holiness and happiness. God hath joined them together; none can put them asunder. <div eID="gen19608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19609" type="x-p"/> But he that trusteth in the Lord - Such a person is both safe and happy.
entries.1374fbcedef6e17d4426124eb4e9b26162ab120f: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen19609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19610" type="x-p"/> Be glad - and rejoice - Let every righteous soul rejoice and glory, but let it be in the Lord. Man was made for happiness, but his happiness must be founded on holiness: and holiness, as it comes from God, must be retained by continual union with him. Probably this verse belongs to the next Psalm, and was originally its first verse.  <chapter eID="Ps.32"/> <div eID="gen19610" type="x-p"/>

entries.5ff141d0cc0d5a63a61827502f01055858f6c5fc: <div eID="gen9365" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Way to the Forgiveness of Sins</title> <div sID="gen9366" type="x-p"/> There are several prominent marks by which this Psalm is coupled with the preceding (vid., <hi type="italic">Symbolae</hi> §52). In both Psalms, with the word אמרתּי, the psalmist looks back upon some fact of his spiritual life; and both close with an exhortation to the godly, which stands in the relation of a general inference to the whole Psalm. But in other respects the two Psalms differ. For Ps 31 is a prayer under circumstances of outward distress, and <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference> is a didactic Psalm, concerning the way of penitence which leads to the forgiveness of sins; it is the second of the seven <hi type="italic">Psalmi paenitentiales </hi>of the church, and Augustine’s favourite Psalm. We might take Augustine’s words as its motto: <hi type="italic">intelligentia prima est ut te noris peccatorem</hi>. The poet bases it upon his own personal experience, and then applies the general teaching which he deduces from it, to each individual in the church of God. For a whole year after his adultery David was like one under sentence of condemnation. In the midst of this fearful anguish of soul he composed Ps 51, whereas <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference> was composed after his deliverance from this state of mind. The former was written in the very midst of the penitential struggle; the latter after he had recovered his inward peace. The theme of this Psalm is the precious treasure which he brought up out of that abyss of spiritual distress, viz., the doctrine of the blessedness of forgiveness, the sincere and unreserved confession of sin as the way to it, and the protection of God in every danger, together with joy in God, as its fruits. <div eID="gen9366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9367" type="x-p"/> In the signification <hi type="italic">psalmus didascalicus s. informatorius</hi> (Reuchlin: <hi type="italic">ut si liceret dicere intellectificum vel resipiscentificum</hi>), משׂכּי would after all be as appropriate a designation as we could have for this Psalm which teachers the way of salvation. This meaning, however, cannot be sustained. It is improbable that משׂכּיל, which, in all other instances, signifies <hi type="italic">intelligens</hi>, should, as a technical term, mean <hi type="italic">intelligentem faciens</hi>; because the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. השׂכּיל, in the causative meaning “to impart understanding,” occurs only in solitary instances (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Psa 32:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.11">Pro 21:11</reference>) in the Hebrew of the period before the Exile, and only came into common use in the later language (in Daniel, Chronicles, and Nehemiah). But, that which is decisive against the meaning “a didactic poem” is the fact, that among the thirteen Psalms which are inscribed משׂיל, there are only two (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference> and Ps 78) which can be regarded as didactic poems. Ps 45 is called, in addition, שׁיר ידידת, and <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.7">Psa 142:1-7</reference>, תּפּלּה, two names which ill accord with a didactic intention and plan. Even <reference osisRef="Ps.47.8">Psa 47:8</reference>, a passage of importance in the determining of the right idea of the word, in which משׂיל occurs as an accusative of the object, excludes the meaning “didactic poem.” Ewald observes (<hi type="italic">Dichter des Alten Bundes</hi>, i. 31) that “in <reference osisRef="Ps.47.8">Psa 47:8</reference> we have the safest guide to the correct meaning of the word; in this passage משׂיל stands side by side with זמּר as a more exact definition of the singing and there can be no doubt, that an <hi type="italic">intelligent</hi>, melodious song must be equivalent to <hi type="italic">choice</hi> or <hi type="italic">delicate</hi>, skillfully composed song.” But in all other cases, משׂיל is only found as an attribute of persons, because it is not that which makes prudent, but that which is itself intelligent, that is so named. Even in <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.22">2Ch 30:22</reference>, where allusion is made to the <hi type="italic">Maskı̂l</hi> Psalms, it is the Levite musicians themselves who are called (שׂכל טוב) המשׂכילים (i.e., those who play skillfully with delicate tact). Thus then we are driven to the Hiphil meaning of pensive meditation in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.7">Psa 106:7</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.41.2">Psa 41:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.20">Pro 16:20</reference>; so that משׂכּיל signifies that which meditates, then meditation, just like מכבּיר, that which multiplies, and then fulness; משׁחית, that which destroys, and then destruction. From the <hi type="italic">Maskı̂l</hi> Psalms, as e.g., from <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.7">Psa 54:1-7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.7">Psa 142:1-7</reference>, we cannot discover anything special as to the technical meaning or use of the word. The word means just <hi type="italic">pia meditatio</hi>, a devout meditation, and nothing more.
entries.d1fe4e192037435b549e062de960f9da73735c81: <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.2">Psa 32:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9368" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins with the celebration of the happiness of the man who experiences God’s justifying grace, when he gives himself up unreservedly to Him. Sin is called פּשׁע, as being a breaking loose or tearing away from God; חטאה, as a deviation from that which is well-pleasing to God; עון, as a perversion, distortion, misdeed. The forgiveness of sin is styled נשׂא (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">Exo 34:7</reference>), as a lifting up and taking away, αἴρειν and ἀφαιρεῖν, <reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">Exo 34:7</reference>; כּסּה (<reference osisRef="Ps.85.3">Psa 85:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pro 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.4.5">Neh 4:5</reference>), as a covering, so that it becomes invisible to God, the Holy One, and is as though it had never taken place; לא חשׁב (<reference osisRef="2Sam.19.20">2Sa 19:20</reference>, cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥsb</hi>, to number, reckon, ου ̓ λογίζεσθαι, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.6-Rom.4.9">Rom 4:6-9</reference>), as a non-imputing; the δικαιοσύνη χωρὶς ἔργων is here distinctly expressed. The justified one is called נשׂוּי־פּשׁע, as being one who is exempted from transgression, <hi type="italic">praevaricatione levatus</hi> (Ges. §135, 1); נשׂוּי, instead of נשׁא, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Isa 33:24</reference>, is intended to rhyme with כּסוּי (which is the <hi type="italic">part</hi>. to כּסּה, just as בּרוּך is the participle to כּרך); vid., on Isa 22:13. One “covered of sin” is one over whose sin lies the covering of expiation (כּפּר, root כף, to cover, cogn. Arab. <hi type="italic">gfr , chfr , chmr , gmr</hi>) before the holy eyes of God. The third designation is an attributive clause: “to whom Jahve doth not reckon misdeed,” inasmuch as He, on the contrary, regards it as discharged or as settled. He who is thus justified, however, is only he in whose spirit there is no רמיּה, no deceit, which denies and hides, or extenuates and excuses, this or that favourite sin. One such sin designedly retained is a secret ban, which stands in the way of justification.
entries.cce5de27af5eec2ac2a09fbf1c16b36038a1d0f2: <reference osisRef="Ps.32.3-Ps.32.5">Psa 32:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen9368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9369" type="x-p"/> For, as his own experience has taught the poet, he who does not in confession pour out all his corruption before God, only tortures himself until he unburdens himself of his secret curse. Since <reference osisRef="Ps.32.3">Psa 32:3</reference> by itself cannot be regarded as the reason for the proposition just laid down, כּי signifies either “because, <hi type="italic">quod</hi>” (e.g., <reference osisRef="Prov.22.22">Pro 22:22</reference>) or “when, <hi type="italic">quum</hi>” (Jdg 16:16; Hos 11:10. The שׁאגה was an outburst of the tortures which his accusing conscience prepared for him. The more he strove against confessing, the louder did conscience speak; and while it was not in his power to silence this inward voice, in which the wrath of God found utterance, he cried the whole day, viz., for help; but while his heart was still unbroken, he cried yet received no answer. He cried all day long, for God’s punishing right hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">Psa 38:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.11">Psa 39:11</reference>) lay heavey upon him day and night; the feeling of divine wrath left him no rest, cf. Job 33:14. A fire burned within him which threatened completely to devour him. The expression is בּחרבני (like בעשׂן in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.20">Psa 37:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.4">Psa 102:4</reference>), without כ, inasmuch as the fears which burn fiercely within him even to his heart and, as it were, scorch him up, he directly calls the droughts of summer. The בּ is the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of the state or condition, in connection with which the change, i.e., degeneration (<reference osisRef="Job.20.14">Job 20:14</reference>), took place; for <hi type="italic">mutare in aliquid</hi> is expressed by הפך ל. The ל (which Saadia and others have mistaken) in לשׁדּי is part of the root; לשׁד (from לשׁד, Arab. <hi type="italic">lsd</hi>, to suck), inflected after the analogy of גּמל and the like, signifies <hi type="italic">succus</hi>. In the summer-heat of anxiety his vital moisture underwent a change: it burned and dried up. Here the music becomes louder and does its part in depicting these torments of the awakened conscience in connection with a heart that still remains unbroken. In spite of this διάψαλμα, however, the historical connection still retains sufficient influence to give אודיעך the force of the imperfect (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.30.9">Psa 30:9</reference>): “I made known my sin and my guilt did I not cover up (כּסּה used here as in <reference osisRef="Prov.27.13">Pro 27:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job 31:33</reference>); I made the resolve: I will confess my transgressions to the Lord (הודה = חתודּה, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.6">Neh 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.2">Neh 9:2</reference>; elsewhere construed with the accusative, vid., <reference osisRef="Prov.28.13">Pro 28:13</reference>) - then Thou forgavest,” etc. Hupfeld is inclined to place אמרתי before חטאתי אודיעך, by which אודיעך and אודה would become futures; but ועוני לא כסיתי sounds like an assertion of a fact, not the statement of an intention, and ואתה נשׂאת is the natural continuation of the אמרתי which immediately precedes. The form ואתה נשׂאת is designedly used instead of ותּשּׂא. Simultaneously with his confession of sin, made <hi type="italic">fide supplice</hi>, came also the absolution: then Thou forgavest the guilt (עון, misdeed, as a deed and also as a matter of fact, i.e., guilt contracted, and penance or punishment, cf. <reference osisRef="Lam.4.6">Lam 4:6</reference>; Zec 14:19) of my sin. <hi type="italic">Vox nondum est in ore</hi>, says Augustine, <hi type="italic">et vulnus sanatur in corde</hi>. The סלה here is the antithesis of the former one. There we have a shrill lament over the sinner who tortures himself in vain, here the clear tones of joy at the blessed experience of one who pours forth his soul to God - a musical Yea and Amen to the great truth of justifying grace.
entries.da44f02a144a14e5dc4cc50b67535a306e61dbcb: <reference osisRef="Ps.32.6-Ps.32.7">Psa 32:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen9369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9370" type="x-p"/> For this mercy, which is provided for every sinner who repents and confesses his sin, let then, every חסיד, who longs for חסד, turn in prayer to Jahve לעת מצא, at the time (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.10">Psa 21:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.22">1Ch 12:22</reference>; cf. בּעת, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.8">Isa 49:8</reference>) when He, and His mercy, is to be found (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.29">Deu 4:29</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.29.13">Jer 29:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6">Isa 55:6</reference>, בּהמּצאו). This hortatory wish is followed by a promissory assurance. The fact of לשׁטף מים רבּים being virtually a protasis: <hi type="italic">quam inundant aquae magnae</hi> (ל of the time), which separates רק from אליו, prohibits our regarding רק as belonging to אליו in this instance, although like אף, אך, גּם, and פּן, רק is also placed <hi type="italic">per hypallage</hi> at the head of the clause (as in <reference osisRef="Prov.13.10">Pro 13:10</reference> : with pride there is only contention), even when belonging to a part of the clause that follows further on. The restrictive meaning of רק here, as is frequently the case (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deu 4:6</reference>; Jdg 14:16; 1Ki 21:25, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.91.8">Psa 91:8</reference>), has passed over to the affirmative: <hi type="italic">certo quum</hi>, etc. Inundation or flooding is an exemplificative description of the divine judgment (cf. <reference osisRef="Nah.1.8">Nah 1:8</reference>); <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference></hi> is a brief form of expressing the promise which is expanded in Ps 91. In <reference osisRef="Ps.32.7">Psa 32:7</reference>, David confirms it from his own experience. The assonance in מצּר תּצּרני (Thou wilt preserve me, so that צר, <hi type="italic">angustum</hi> = <hi type="italic">angustiae</hi>, does not come upon me, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.143">Psa 119:143</reference>) is not undesigned; and after תצרני comes רני, just like כלו after בהיכלו in Psa 29:9. There is no sufficient ground for setting aside רני, with Houbigant and others, as a repetition of the half of the word תצרני. The infinitive רן (<reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job 38:7</reference>) might, like רב, <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. רבּי, חק, <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. חקּי, with equal right be inflected as a substantive; and פּלּט (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.56.8">Psa 56:8</reference>), which is likewise treated as a substantive, cf. נפּץ, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.7">Dan 12:7</reference>, presents, as a genitive, no more difficulty than does דעת in the expression אישׁ דּעת. With songs of deliverance doth Jahve surround him, so that they encompass him on all sides, and on occasion of exulting meets him in whatever direction he turns. The music here again for the third time becomes <hi type="italic">forte</hi>, and that to express the highest feeling of delight.
entries.8afa4ccc286f7f8d74e7b64ae10231ea42ce2114: <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8-Ps.32.10">Psa 32:8-10</reference> <div eID="gen9370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9371" type="x-p"/> It is not Jahve, who here speaks in answer to the words that have been thus far addressed to Him. In this case the person addressed must be the poet, who, however, has already attained the knowledge here treated of. It is he himself who now directly adopts the tone of the teacher (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.34.12">Psa 34:12</reference>). That which David, in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.15">Psa 51:15</reference>, promises to do, he here takes in hand, viz., the instruction of sinners in the way of salvation. It is unnecessary to read איעצך instead of איעצה, as Olshausen does; the suffix of אשׂכּילך and אורך (for אורך) avails also for this third verb, to which עליך עיני, equivalent to שׂם עליך עיני (fixing my eye upon thee, i.e., with sympathising love taking an interest in thee), stands in the relation of a subordinate relative clause. The lxx renders it by ἐπιστηριῶ ἐπὶ σὲ τοὺς ὀφθαλμούς μου, so that it takes יעץ, in accordance with its radical signification <hi type="italic">firmare</hi>, as the <hi type="italic">regens</hi> of עיני (I will fix my eye steadfastly upon thee); but for this there is no support in the general usage of the language. The accents give a still different rendering; they apparently make עיני an <hi type="italic">accus. adverb</hi>. (Since אעצה עליך עיני is transformed from איעצה עליך עיני: I will counsel thee with mine eye; but in every other instance, יעץ על means only a hostile determination against any one, e.g., Isa 7:5. The form of address, without changing its object, passes over, in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Psa 32:9</reference>, into the plural and the expression becomes harsh in perfect keeping with the perverted character which it describes. The sense is on the whole clear: not constrained, but willing obedience is becoming to man, in distinction from an irrational animal which must be led by a bridle drawn through its mouth. The asyndeton clause: like a horse, a mule (פּרד as an animal that is isolated and does not pair; cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">fard</hi>, alone of its kind, single, unlike, the opposite of which is Arab. <hi type="italic">zawj</hi>, a pair, equal number), has nothing remarkable about it, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.35.14">Psa 35:14</reference>; Isa 38:14. But it is not clear what עדיו is intended to mean. We might take it in its usual signification “ornament,” and render “with bit and bridle, its ornament,” and perhaps at once recognise therein an allusion to the senseless servility of the animal, viz., that its ornament is also the means by which it is kept in check, unless עדי, ornament, is perhaps directly equivalent to “harness.” Still the rendering of the lxx is to be respected: <hi type="italic">in camo et fraeno</hi> - as Jerome reproduces it - <hi type="italic">maxilas eorum constringere qui non approximant ad te</hi>. If עדי means jaw, mouth or check, then עדיו לבלום is equivalent to <hi type="italic">ora eorum obturanda sunt</hi> (Ges. §132, rem. 1), which the lxx expressed by ἄγξαι, <hi type="italic">constringe</hi>, or following the <hi type="italic">Cod. Alex.</hi>, ἄγξις (ἄγξεις), <hi type="italic">constringes</hi>. Like Ewald and Hitzig (on <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.7">Eze 16:7</reference>), we may compare with עדי, the cheek, the Arabic <hi type="italic">chadd</hi>, which, being connected with גּדוּד, a furrow, signifies properly the furrow of the face, i.e., the indented part running downwards from the inner corners of the eyes to both sides of the nose, but then by synecdoche the cheek. If `dyw refers to the mouth or jaws, then it looks as if בּל קרב אליך must be translated: in order that they may not come too near thee, viz., to hurt thee (Targ., Syriac, Rashi, etc.); but this rendering does not produce any point of comparison corresponding to the context of this Psalm. Therefore, it is rather to be rendered: otherwise there is no coming near to thee. This interpretation takes the emphasis of the בל into account, and assumes that, according to a usage of the language that is without further support, one might, for instance, say: בּל לכתּי שׁמּה, “I will never go thither.” In <reference osisRef="Prov.23.17">Pro 23:17</reference>, בל also includes within itself the verb to be. So here: by no means an approaching to thee, i.e., there is, if thou dost not bridle them, no approaching or coming near to thee. These words are not addressed to God, but to man, who is obliged to use harsh and forcible means in taming animals, and can only thus keep them under his control and near to him. In the antitype, it is the sinner, who will not come to God, although God only is his help, and who, as David has learned by experience, must first of all endure inward torture, before he comes to a right state of mind. This agonising life of the guilty conscience which the ungodly man leads, is contrasted in <reference osisRef="Ps.32.10">Psa 32:10</reference> with the mercy which encompasses on all sides him, who trusts in God. רבּים, in accordance with the treatment of this adjective as if it were a numeral (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.89.51">Psa 89:51</reference>), is an attributive or adjective placed before its noun. The final clause might be rendered: mercy encompasses him; but the <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> and <reference osisRef="Ps.32.7">Psa 32:7</reference> favour the rendering: with mercy doth He encompass him.

PSALM 32.
David having largely and painfully experienced what a miserable thing it is to feel God’s hand heavy on account of sin, exclaims that the highest and best part of a happy life consists in this, that God forgives a man’s guilt, and receives him graciously into his favor. After giving thanks for pardon obtained, he invites others to fellowship with him in his happiness, showing, by his own example, the means by which this may be obtained.
A Psalm of David giving instruction.
The title of this psalm gives some idea of its subject. Some think that the Hebrew word משכיל, maskil, which we have rendered giving instruction,
“Pour lequel nous avons traduit, Donnant instruction.” — Fr.
is taken from verse 7th;
Where it is said, “I will instruct thee and teach thee.”
but it is more accurate to consider it as a title given to the psalm in accordance with its whole scope and subject matter. David, after enduring long and dreadful torments, when God was severely trying him, by showing him the tokens of his wrath, having at length obtained favor, applies this evidence of the divine goodness for his own benefit, and the benefit of the whole Church, that from it he may teach himself and them what constitutes the chief point of salvation. All men must necessarily be either in miserable torment, or, which is worse, forgetting themselves and God, must continue in deadly lethargy, until they are persuaded that God is reconciled towards them. Hence David here teaches us that the happiness of men consists only in the free forgiveness of sins, for nothing can be more terrible than to have God for our enemy; nor can he be gracious to us in any other way than by pardoning our transgressions.
Psalm 32:1-2
1. Blessed are they whose iniquity is forgiven, and whose transgression is covered. 2. Blessed is the man to whom Jehovah imputeth no sin, and in whose spirit there is no guile.
 
1. Blessed are they whose iniquity is forgiven. This exclamation springs from the fervent affection of the Psalmist’s heart as well as from serious consideration. Since almost the whole world turning away their thoughts from God’s judgment, bring upon themselves a fatal forgetfulness, and intoxicate themselves with deceitful pleasures; David, as if he had been stricken with the fear of God’s wrath, that he might betake himself to Divine mercy, awakens others also to the same exercise, by declaring distinctly and loudly that those only are blessed to whom God is reconciled, so as to acknowledge those for his children whom he might justly treat as his enemies. Some are so blinded with hypocrisy and pride, and some with such gross contempt of God, that they are not at all anxious in seeking forgiveness, but all acknowledge that they need forgiveness; nor is there a man in existence whose conscience does not accuse him at God’s judgment-seat, and gall him with many stings. This confession, accordingly, that all need forgiveness, because no man is perfect, and that then only is it well with us when God pardons our sins, nature herself extorts even from wicked men. But in the meantime, hypocrisy shuts the eyes of multitudes, while others are so deluded by a perverse carnal security, that they are touched either with no feelings of Divine wrath, or with only a frigid feeling of it.
From this proceeds a twofold error: first, that such men make light of their sins, and reflect not on the hundredth part of their danger from God’s indignation; and, secondly, that they invent frivolous expiations to free themselves from guilt and to purchase the favor of God. Thus in all ages it has been everywhere a prevailing opinion, that although all men are infected with sin, they are at the same time adorned with merits which are calculated to procure for them the favor of God, and that although they provoke his wrath by their crimes, they have expiations and satisfactions in readiness to obtain their absolution. This delusion of Satan is equally common among Papists, Turks, Jews, and other nations. Every man, therefore, who is not carried away by the furious madness of Popery, will admit the truth of this statement, that men are in a wretched state unless God deal mercifully with them by not laying their sins to their charge. But David goes farther, declaring that the whole life of man is subjected to God’s wrath and curse, except in so far as he vouchsafes of his own free grace to receive them into his favor; of which the Spirit who spake by David is an assured interpreter and witness to us by the mouth of Paul, (Romans 4:6.) Had Paul not used this testimony, never would his readers have penetrated the real meaning of the prophet; for we see that the Papists, although they chant in their temples, “Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven,” etc., yet pass over it as if it were some common saying and of little importance. But with Paul, this is the full definition of the righteousness of faith; as if the prophet had said, Men are then only blessed when they are freely reconciled to God, and counted as righteous by him. The blessedness, accordingly, that David celebrates utterly destroys the righteousness of works. The device of a partial righteousness with which Papists and others delude themselves is mere folly; and even among those who are destitute of the light of heavenly doctrine, no one will be found so mad as to arrogate a perfect righteousness to himself, as appears from the expiations, washings, and other means of appeasing God, which have always been in use among all nations. But yet they do not hesitate to obtrude their virtues upon God, just as if by them they had acquired of themselves a great part of their blessedness.
David, however, prescribes a very different order, namely, that in seeking happiness, all should begin with the principle, that God cannot be reconciled to those who are worthy of eternal destruction in any other way than by freely pardoning them, and bestowing upon them his favor. And justly does he declare that if mercy is withheld from them, all men must be utterly wretched and accursed; for if all men are naturally prone only to evil, until they are regenerated, their whole previous life, it is obvious, must be hateful and loathsome in the sight of God. Besides, as even after regeneration, no work which men perform can please God unless he pardons the sin which mingles with it, they must be excluded from the hope of salvation. Certainly nothing will remain for them but cause for the greatest terror. That the works of the saints are unworthy of reward because they are spotted with stains, seems a hard saying to the Papists. But, in this they betray their gross ignorance in estimating, according to their own conceptions, the judgment of God, in whose eyes the very brightness of the stars is but darkness. Let this therefore remain an established doctrine, that as we are only accounted righteous before God by the free remission of sins, this is the gate of eternal salvation; and, accordingly, that they only are blessed who rely upon God’s mercy. We must bear in mind the contrast which I have already mentioned between believers who, embracing the remission of sins, rely upon the grace of God alone, and all others who neglect to betake themselves to the sanctuary of Divine grace.
Moreover, when David thrice repeats the same thing, this is no vain repetition. It is indeed sufficiently evident of itself that the man must be blessed whose iniquity is forgiven; but experience teaches us how difficult it is to become persuaded of this in such a manner as to have it thoroughly fixed in our hearts. The great majority, as I have already shown you, entangled by devices of their own, put away from them, as far as they can, the terrors of conscience and all fear of Divine wrath. They have, no doubt, a desire to be reconciled to God; and yet they shun the sight of him, rather than seek his grace sincerely and with all their hearts. Those, on the other hand, whom God has truly awakened so as to be affected with a lively sense of their misery, are so constantly agitated and disquieted that it is difficult to restore peace to their minds. They taste indeed God’s mercy, and endeavor to lay hold of it, and yet they are frequently abashed or made to stagger under the manifold assaults which are made upon them. The two reasons for which the Psalmist insists so much on the subject of the forgiveness of sins are these, - that he may, on the one hand, raise up those who are fallen asleep, inspire the careless with thoughtfulness, and quicken the dull; and that he may, on the other hand, tranquillise fearful and anxious minds with an assured and steady confidence. To the former, the doctrine may be applied in this manner: ”What mean ye, O ye unhappy men! that one or two stings of conscience do not disturb you? Suppose that a certain limited knowledge of your sins is not sufficient to strike you with terror, yet how preposterous is it to continue securely asleep, while you are overwhelmed with an immense load of sins?” And this repetition furnishes not a little comfort and confirmation to the feeble and fearful. As doubts are often coming upon them, one after another, it is not sufficient that they are victorious in one conflict only. That despair, therefore, may not overwhelm them amidst the various perplexing thoughts with which they are agitated, the Holy Spirit confirms and ratifies the remission of sins with many declarations.
It is now proper to weigh the particular force of the expressions here employed. Certainly the remission which is here treated of does not agree with satisfactions. God, in lifting off or taking away sins, and likewise in covering and not imputing them, freely pardons them. On this account the Papists, by thrusting in their satisfactions and works of supererogation as they call them, bereave themselves of this blessedness. Besides, David applies these words to complete forgiveness. The distinction, therefore, which the Papists here make between the remission of the punishment and of the fault, by which they make only half a pardon, is not at all to the purpose. Now, it is necessary to consider to whom this happiness belongs, which may be easily gathered from the circumstance of the time. When David was taught that he was blessed through the mercy of God alone, he was not an alien from the church of God; on the contrary, he had profited above many in the fear and service of God, and in holiness of life, and had exercised himself in all the duties of godliness. And even after making these advances in religion, God so exercised him, that he placed the alpha and omega of his salvation in his gratuitous reconciliation to God. Nor is it without reason that Zacharias, in his song, represents “the knowledge of salvation” as consisting in knowing “the remission of sins,” (Luke 1:77.) The more eminently that any one excels in holiness, the farther he feels himself from perfect righteousness, and the more clearly he perceives that he can trust in nothing but the mercy of God alone. Hence it appears, that those are grossly mistaken who conceive that the pardon of sin is necessary only to the beginning of righteousness. As believers are every day involved in many faults, it will profit them nothing that they have once entered the way of righteousness, unless the same grace which brought them into it accompany them to the last step of their life. Does any one object, that they are elsewhere said to be blessed “who fear the Lord,” “who walk in his ways,” “who are upright in heart,” etc., the answer is easy, namely, that as the perfect fear of the Lord, the perfect observance of his law, and perfect uprightness of heart, are nowhere to be found, all that the Scripture anywhere says, concerning blessedness, is founded upon the free favor of God, by which he reconciles us to himself.

                  <ns0:p n="8">8. I will instruct <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">This and the next Verse are the Words, Either, 1. Of God; whom <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> brings in as returning this Answer to his Prayers, and the pro<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>lar Favours from God, and having declared what the Godly would do up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on that <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap>rtakes to instruct the wick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, what thy should do. Which he doth, Partly, to express his thankfulness to God, for delivering himself and his Zeal, to advance the Honour and Service of God in the World; Partly, as an Act of Justice, that he might make some amends to those whom <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e had injured and provoke them to Repen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance, whom by his sins he had Scandalized; and either drawn to sin<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or incouraged and hardened in sin, which he was O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bliged and did promise to do, upon this, or the like Oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casion, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 51. 13. and Partly, for the discharge of his Of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fice and Duty, as he was both a King and a Prophet, and a good Man; in all which Capacities, he was Obliged to in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deavour the Conversion and Salvation of sinners.</ns0:note> thee <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Thee Oh sinner, whosoever thou art, who hast no understanding, but art a wicked Man, as the two following Verses explain it. He speaks this to the Generality of impenitent Sinners, as the next Verse shews, which begins in the plural Number, <ns0:hi>Be not ye,</ns0:hi> &c Onely he expresseth it here singularly, as appealing and ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plying himself particularly, to the Conscience of every indivi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dual Person, which he thought the most effectual way of pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding, as he had found in himself, when <ns0:hi>Nathan</ns0:hi> applyed his indefinite Discourse to him, saying, <ns0:hi>Thou art the Man.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) In which thou oughtest to walk; the Future Tense oft noting a mans Duty as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 20. 9. <ns0:hi>Mal.</ns0:hi> 1 6.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb: <ns0:hi>I will Counsel</ns0:hi> thee: <ns0:hi>mine eye shall be upon thee.</ns0:hi>

Or, the Words may be thus rendred, <ns0:hi>I will give</ns0:hi> thee <ns0:hi>Counsel, mine Eye</ns0:hi> shall be <ns0:hi>upon thee,</ns0:hi> as it is more fully ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 44. 21. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 24. 6. and 40. 4.                   <ns0:p n="9">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:445" />9. Be ye not as the horse, <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> as the mule<ns0:note place="margin">

Poole.heading:
PSAL. XXXII. 
                     Or, A Psalm of David, giving instruction.
                      
                     A Psalm of David, Maschil Or, an Instructer. This Psalm is most fitly so called, because it was Composed for the information of the Church, in that most important Doctrine, Concerning the way to true Blessedness..
